title: SEAT Ateca side mirror
subtitle: Redesign of the exterior mirror of a family SUV
deck: A mirror that folds itself before it hits something, and keeps the driver seeing when it does.
role: Worked across the whole project. Led the regulatory analysis (ECE R46) in the product-analysis phase and most of the development phase: analysis and redesign of the new circuit, the material specification manual, the mould machining roadmap and the justification of the selected material. Led the final renders.
team: Ainhoa Alonso, Mikel Arnao, Maren Leston, Ane Pelayo, Garazi Portillo
tools: SolidWorks, SolidWorks Simulation, CES EduPack, KeyShot, resin 3D printing

stats.label: energy for a 50-minute, 25 km trip, inside the 4–8 Wh target
deflection under aerodynamic load at 180 km/h
new components: folding motor, camera, radar, ultrasonic sensor, blind-spot LED

hero.caption: Final render of the redesigned mirror with dynamic LED indicator.

sections.title: Context and brief
paragraphs: The Ateca is a compact family SUV. Of three archetypes, the team chose Maite, a mother who picks her children up from school on a narrow, chaotic street and is afraid of clipping the mirror while manoeuvring.
Brief: keep the Ateca family look, remove that stress with assistance systems and stay fully within ECE Regulation 46.

figures.caption: Storyboard of the school pick-up used to find the pain point.

sections.title: Research
paragraphs: A benchmark of six rival SUV mirrors, mapped by price and technology, showed no affordable high-tech option. The regulatory study set the hard limits:
list: Minimum edge radius of 2.5 mm on housing and glass
Class III field of view: 20 m long and 4 m wide
No part above 2 m from the ground; vehicle width with mirrors under 2.55 m
Heated glass and LED indicator compliant with EU electrical and lighting rules

sections.title: Concepts
paragraphs: Brainstorming and four-step sketching produced three preliminary designs: one with a rain deflector, an aerodynamic one with blind-spot indicator, and a robust one with a hidden auxiliary mirror. A Pugh matrix chose concept 2, positive on viability, aesthetics, function and regulations.

sections.title: Development
paragraphs: An ultrasonic sensor folds the mirror when an obstacle gets close; a camera streams to the central screen while it is folded; a radar drives a blind-spot LED. The circuit was redesigned at 12 V with the sensors in parallel to the EFB battery.
SolidWorks Simulation checked aerodynamic load, a 33 J pedestrian impact, fatigue at one million cycles, 500 N vertical and 300 N lateral loads, modal and thermal behaviour.

sections.title: Specification
paragraphs: The material specification manual turned functional, mechanical, thermal and chemical requirements into CES EduPack constraints and performance indices. The top five candidates were weighted after min–max normalisation; PCTFE was chosen for its UV, humidity and chemical resistance. Machining roadmaps were written for both mould halves.

sections.title: Result
paragraphs: A 1:1 aesthetic prototype printed in resin, filled, primed and painted, with an amber indicator and a laser-cut mirror on a hand-shaped curved base.

figures.caption: Render of the mirror glass and camera.

sections.title: Reflection
paragraphs: Simulation in SolidWorks went beyond the syllabus. The next step would be a functional prototype to test ergonomics, tolerances and assembly that virtual tools do not show.
